narrativeReportMd:
# unsignedInt R4-to-R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
No definite hard instance-breaking change was found for conformant R4 `unsignedInt` values. The artifact identity and content model are preserved. The material local changes are computable metadata changes on `unsignedInt.value`: R6 makes the unsigned integer range explicit and shifts value typing metadata toward numeric `unsignedInt`/`System.Integer` semantics.

## Scope
This assessment is scoped to the `unsignedInt` primitive datatype StructureDefinition. Inherited changes from `Element`, `Extension`, `integer`, and `PrimitiveType` are excluded as local findings under the inherited/base-artifact rule.

## Main migration themes
The main risk is not a new element or a wire-format rename. It is stricter or more precise primitive value handling by validators and generators that consume R6 ElementDefinition metadata. Systems that treated R4 `unsignedInt` as an unconstrained non-negative decimal string, or generated string-valued APIs from the R4 snapshot metadata, may need to tighten validation and numeric typing.

## Highest-impact findings
The highest-impact finding is the explicit R6 `0..2147483647` value range. Correct R4 implementations should already inherit the 32-bit integer ceiling from `integer`, but the R4 `unsignedInt` StructureDefinition did not state that limit on `unsignedInt.value` itself. That creates a potential migration break for lenient validators or generated schemas that accepted oversized non-negative values.

## Findings requiring human review
The range finding deserves human review because an official diff or rendered narrative would help determine whether the R6 bounds are intended as a new constraint or as a computable correction of the existing integer-derived semantics.

## Backward-compatible design observations
Both local changes appear aimed at making the primitive's semantics more computable and consistent. A less disruptive alternative would have been to add explicit advisory metadata while preserving the old string-oriented representation metadata, but that would continue ambiguity for validators and code generators.

## Follow-up analysis
The `integer` datatype and primitive-type hierarchy should be reviewed separately for inherited base behavior. No terminology follow-up is needed because `unsignedInt` has no terminology binding.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: R6 preserves `unsignedInt` identity and element structure, with no definite conformant old-valid/new-invalid instance identified. The top migration concerns are explicit `0..2147483647` bounds, more numeric value type metadata, and implementation-specific generator behavior. Confidence is medium because official narrative/diff evidence would clarify intent and because the R6 snapshot and differential do not present the value type identically.
summary.migrationThemesMd: Migration should focus on validators, schemas, and generated primitive wrappers rather than resource transforms. Existing data using non-negative 32-bit integers should carry forward unchanged. Data stores or APIs that allowed oversized non-negative values, or represented all `unsignedInt` values as arbitrary strings based on R4 snapshot metadata, should be checked and remediated.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: The structural comparison is high confidence because both local StructureDefinitions are present and small. Impact confidence is medium because a fully conformant R4 interpretation already inherits 32-bit integer bounds from `integer`, while some tooling may have relied on the less explicit R4 `unsignedInt` snapshot/differential.

findings.title: R6 explicitly constrains unsignedInt.value to 0..2147483647

oldState.summary: The R4 unsignedInt StructureDefinition required a non-negative lexical form but did not declare unsignedInt-specific minValueUnsignedInt or maxValueUnsignedInt on unsignedInt.value.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 `unsignedInt.value` carried the non-negative regex `[0]|([1-9][0-9]*)`. The assigned `unsignedInt` StructureDefinition did not itself include explicit `minValueUnsignedInt` or `maxValueUnsignedInt` fields, although the `integer` base datatype did define a 32-bit integer range.

newState.summary: The R6 unsignedInt differential declares minValueUnsignedInt 0 and maxValueUnsignedInt 2147483647 on unsignedInt.value, while retaining the same non-negative regex.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 makes the permitted numeric range computable directly from the `unsignedInt` differential: values must be at least 0 and no greater than 2147483647.

facts.note: The lexical non-negative constraint did not change.
This supporting fact is inherited from integer and is not counted as a local unsignedInt finding.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The same element id and path `unsignedInt.value` exist in both versions; the change is a local addition of value-limit metadata in the R6 differential.

impact.impactRationaleMd: For a fully conformant R4 validator that applies the `integer` base datatype, oversized values above 2147483647 should already be invalid, so no definite hard instance break is proven. The risk is still material because the R4 `unsignedInt` StructureDefinition did not state the upper bound locally; validators, JSON schemas, database columns, or generated code that used only the leaf datatype metadata may have accepted arbitrary-size non-negative integers. R6 makes rejection of those values much more likely.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The primary risk is validation or migration failure for out-of-range numeric data. No direct clinical safety issue was identified for conformant in-range values.

justification.inferredGoal: Make the unsignedInt numeric range explicit and computable on the datatype specialization.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep the R4 leaf definition without formal unsignedInt min/max and rely on inherited integer semantics plus advisory guidance.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The inferred R6 goal is reasonable: make the `unsignedInt` value range explicit and computable on the datatype itself. Because conformant R4 semantics already inherit the 32-bit `integer` ceiling, the added R6 min/max mainly breaks lenient or leaf-only tooling rather than known valid R4 instances. That level of breakage is probably proportionate to the interoperability benefit of a formal base constraint.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design could have left `unsignedInt.value` with only the R4 non-negative regex, relied on the `integer` base range, and added narrative guidance, type-characteristics metadata, or warning-level validation advice. That alternative would cover common in-range data and reduce churn for permissive validators, but it is only partial: oversized values would remain inconsistently handled, and tooling would still need to infer a normative range from outside the leaf datatype.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: This would preserve lax R4 tooling but would not give R6 deterministic base validation for the unsignedInt range.

evidence.detail: R4 unsignedInt.value has the non-negative regex but no minValueUnsignedInt or maxValueUnsignedInt.
R6 unsignedInt.value declares minValueUnsignedInt 0 and maxValueUnsignedInt 2147483647.
The R4 integer base datatype already has 32-bit min and max values, which limits confidence that the R6 unsignedInt max is truly new semantically.

examples.examplesMd: No definitive conformant R4 old-valid/new-invalid example was identified. A value such as `2147483648` is illustrative of the migration risk for lenient R4 tooling, but it is not claimed here as valid under a fully conformant R4 interpretation that applies the `integer` base range.

findings.narrativeMd: `unsignedInt.value` now has an explicit computable range of `0..2147483647` in the R6 differential. This matters because some R4-era tools may have read the leaf `unsignedInt` definition as only a non-negative regex and may not have enforced the inherited 32-bit integer ceiling. Those tools can encounter new validation failures when moving to R6 metadata.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: The clearest validation effect is for oversized non-negative values. A fully conformant R4 validator should already reject them through the `integer` base, but a validator or generated schema that used only the R4 `unsignedInt` leaf definition could accept them and then reject them under R6. R6-valid values within `0..2147483647` remain representable in R4.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Audit persisted and test data for `unsignedInt` values outside `0..2147483647`. Tighten validators, database columns, and generated schemas to the explicit R6 range. If oversized historical values exist, they cannot be losslessly represented as R6 `unsignedInt`; systems should correct the source value, map it to a different datatype or extension where the owning artifact permits that, or reject/quarantine the record.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change is probably justified because it makes an existing integer-derived limit directly computable on the specialized datatype. A backward-compatible alternative would have been advisory guidance rather than a formal value limit, but that would preserve ambiguity and inconsistent validation.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Human review should confirm against the rendered R6 datatype page or official diff whether the explicit max is intended as a normative tightening or as a correction of an omission in the R4 unsignedInt leaf StructureDefinition.

findings.title: Value type metadata shifts from string-oriented representation toward unsignedInt/integer

oldState.summary: R4 snapshot metadata for unsignedInt.value used FHIRPath System.String and a structuredefinition-fhir-type extension valueUrl of string; the R4 differential used System.String with fhir-type unsignedInt.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 exposed mixed metadata for code generators: the snapshot looked string-oriented, while the differential already carried the more specific `unsignedInt` FHIR type extension.

newState.summary: R6 snapshot metadata uses fhir-type unsignedInt, and the R6 differential changes the ElementDefinition type code to FHIRPath System.Integer while keeping XML attribute representation and the same regex.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 metadata is more numeric and datatype-specific. The differential says the primitive value is a FHIRPath `System.Integer`; the snapshot still retains `System.String` as the low-level carrier but identifies the FHIR type as `unsignedInt`.

facts.note: The R6 snapshot and differential differ on this low-level type code.
No XML attribute representation change was found.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The same `unsignedInt.value` element is present in both versions; the delta concerns ElementDefinition type metadata rather than element identity.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The wire-level primitive remains `unsignedInt` with the same element path, cardinality, regex, and XML attribute representation, so conformant instances do not break simply because of this metadata shift. Runtime and code-generation risk is medium for tools that generated string-valued APIs or schemas from the R4 snapshot and will now generate integer-valued APIs from the R6 differential or datatype-specific extension.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The likely effect is parser, serializer, or SDK API mismatch. Business risk comes from migration defects or rejected data at integration boundaries rather than a changed clinical meaning.

justification.inferredGoal: Align primitive value metadata with unsignedInt's numeric semantics and reduce string-vs-integer ambiguity for tooling.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep the R4 string-oriented type code and add separate annotations or guidance for numeric unsignedInt handling.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The goal of aligning computable metadata with `unsignedInt`'s numeric semantics is reasonable, and this finding is a runtime/code-generation compatibility risk rather than a wire-format instance break. R6 still preserves the same element path and primitive representation, while making the datatype-specific numeric intent clearer. The remaining breakage for tools that treated the R4 snapshot as a direct string API is probably justified by reducing long-standing ambiguity.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design could have retained `http://hl7.org/fhirpath/System.String` as the authoritative value type code and expressed numeric handling only through the `structuredefinition-fhir-type` extension, type-characteristics metadata, or generator guidance. That is a real but incomplete alternative: it protects older generators, but it does not meet the R6 goal as cleanly because tools would still see multiple signals about whether the primitive value is string-like or integer-like.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: This would reduce generator churn but would preserve conflicting string-versus-integer signals for validators, SDKs, and FHIRPath-aware tooling.

evidence.detail: R4 snapshot unsignedInt.value type code is FHIRPath System.String and the fhir-type extension valueUrl is string.
R4 differential already identifies the FHIR type extension as unsignedInt while keeping the type code as FHIRPath System.String.
R6 snapshot unsignedInt.value keeps FHIRPath System.String as the low-level type code but changes the fhir-type extension to unsignedInt.
R6 differential unsignedInt.value changes the type code to FHIRPath System.Integer.

migrationExampleJson.generatorPolicy: Expose unsignedInt values as bounded non-negative integer APIs while preserving FHIR primitive extension/id handling for the element wrapper.

examples.examplesMd: The example is a generator policy rather than a FHIR instance fragment. It highlights that the public API type may change even though the FHIR element path and primitive wrapper behavior remain the same.

findings.narrativeMd: `unsignedInt.value` metadata is more numeric in R6. This can surprise tooling that treats primitive ElementDefinition type codes as direct language types. A generator that emitted a string property from the R4 snapshot may emit an integer property from the R6 differential, affecting parser coercion, serializer tests, database schemas, and FHIRPath evaluation assumptions.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: This finding is not a hard instance validation break by itself. Existing in-range `unsignedInt` values have the same element name and lexical pattern. The compatibility risk is runtime-facing: generated classes, JSON schema, OpenAPI models, or validators may change the expected host-language type from string-like to integer-like.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Review generated SDKs, schema artifacts, and primitive serializers for `unsignedInt`. Ensure they enforce integer semantics and `0..2147483647` bounds while still supporting primitive extension/id wrappers. Regression tests should cover JSON numeric values, XML attribute serialization, primitive extensions, zero, one, the upper bound, and out-of-range values.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change appears justified as a metadata correction toward the datatype's actual numeric semantics. The less-breaking alternative of keeping string-oriented metadata would avoid some generator churn but would leave the datatype ambiguous and less useful for validation.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: The R6 snapshot still reports `System.String` while the R6 differential reports `System.Integer`; implementation impact depends on which representation a tool treats as authoritative.

checkedNoMaterialChange.notesMd: Canonical URL, id, name, kind, type, abstract flag, derivation, and immediate baseDefinition are preserved. The R6 counterpart is present at `StructureDefinition-unsignedInt.json`.
Both snapshots contain the same local element paths: `unsignedInt`, `unsignedInt.id`, `unsignedInt.extension`, and `unsignedInt.value`.
`unsignedInt` has no Reference-typed elements or targetProfiles.
No terminology bindings are present, so no binding strength, value set, or code expansion change applies.

No local unsignedInt-specific invariant was added or removed. Inherited `Element`/`Extension` constraint text and XPath metadata differences are excluded from local findings under the base-artifact scope rule.
No fixed value, pattern value, or defaultValue appears on the local unsignedInt elements.
All local elements remain `isModifier: false` where the flag is present; no modifier reason change affects unsignedInt.
All local elements remain `isSummary: false` where the flag is present.
No slicing is present in either unsignedInt StructureDefinition.

The root definition remains `An integer with a value that is not negative (e.g. >= 0)`. Administrative description wording changed from `Base StructureDefinition for unsignedInt type` to `unsignedInt type`, but that does not change datatype semantics.
An R6 `unsignedInt` value within `0..2147483647` is representable as the same `unsignedInt` primitive in R4. No R6-only child element or code system value was added.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: R6 adds type-characteristics metadata for range and length
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The added `structuredefinition-type-characteristics` extensions are annotations on the StructureDefinition and do not add a new instance element or change the wire representation.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Tooling that uses type-characteristics metadata may gain a more direct way to identify `unsignedInt` as a ranged primitive; this should complement, not replace, value-limit enforcement.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: R6 updates administrative metadata without changing identity
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: R6 adds or updates administrative fields such as generated narrative text, `experimental: false`, jurisdiction, publisher/contact details, and package metadata. The canonical identity and primitive datatype role remain unchanged.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Metadata harvesters may see new administrative fields, but instance validation and conversion do not need a data transform for these changes.
